extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and human-rights practitioners interested in Angola
extracted.subtask_description: A country-level survey of civil, political, economic, and social rights in Angola, summarizing statutory guarantees and documented violations across specific rights areas. Useful for monitoring, reporting, or background research on Angola's human-rights situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic rights / non-discrimination (constitutional guarantees vs enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: While Angola's constitution and law prohibit discrimination based on race, gender, religion, disability, language, or social status, the government has not effectively enforced these prohibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should compare formal legal protections (constitutional and statutory) with enforcement in practice; note examples of weak enforcement and sectors where discrimination persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of expression and media freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Angola's 2010 constitution guarantees the rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, and freedom of the media, but the government has increasingly limited the exercise of these rights via illegal surveillance, arrests, harassment, prosecution for defamation, censorship, and pressure on advertisers leading to self-censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both de jure guarantees and de facto restrictions: surveillance practices, arrests of journalists, incidents of violence against journalists, censorship of state and private media, legal prosecution, and economic pressure on media outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police violence and use of excessive force
rubrics_metrics.description: Security forces have used excessive force resulting in deaths, including arbitrary killings (in 2009 'arbitrarily killed 61 persons') and allegations of off-duty officers shooting and killing individuals with little accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure incidence of deaths and injuries from police actions, presence/absence of prosecutions, reports by Amnesty/HRW, and patterns of impunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of assembly and protest rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the right of assembly is constitutionally guaranteed, demonstrations are frequently disrupted by police; authorities require prior information for gatherings, sometimes forbid areas used for protests, and routinely disallow or heavily monitor gatherings critical of the regime, with organizers subject to arrest or violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legal requirements for assemblies, instances of denial or restriction of locations (e.g., by-laws excluding Independence Square), documented crackdowns on protests, arrests of organizers, and use of teargas/gunfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of religion (registration/licensing rules and practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Angola defines itself as secular and guarantees freedom of conscience and religion, but religious groups must apply for licenses and meet stringent thresholds (2004 Law on Religion: at least 100,000 members and adherents in 12 provinces) for recognition; Islam has been effectively unrecognized with mosques and Islamic centers closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare constitutional guarantees to licensing requirements and documented closures or discriminatory treatment of specific faiths; note official list of 83 recognized groups versus thousands operating illegally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of movement (internal and international travel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutionally permitted freedom of movement is complicated in practice by internal checkpoints where travelers face harassment and extortion, and a rigid system of entry and exit visas complicates international travel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate frequency and nature of checkpoint harassment, extortion claims, and administrative barriers to travel; examine visa/exit controls and their application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption and impunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Corruption is illegal but endemic in government and business and is rarely prosecuted; extortion and bribery are widespread; laws and institutions are often dominated by the president and Council of Ministers, with laws rubber-stamped by the National Assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prevalence of bribery/extortion, enforcement rates, institutional independence, examples of high-level impunity, and impact on other rights (e.g., judicial process, land seizures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property rights and forced evictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2010 constitution declares all land belongs to the state; the government frequently seizes and destroys private homes without fair compensation, conducting large-scale forced evictions (sometimes resulting in deaths) and selling seized land to private companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document legal regime on land ownership, frequency/scale of evictions, compensation practices, and specific incidents (e.g., 2010 incident with seven killed; 2011 eviction of 40 families).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of migrants and expulsions
rubrics_metrics.description: Police have committed rapes and other violent abuses during expulsions of migrants; reports document sexual violence, gang rape, beatings, degrading treatment, arbitrary arrests, denial of due process, especially against Congolese migrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess treatment during roundups and expulsions, incidence of sexual violence and other abuses, official responses/denials, and cooperation with UN on expulsions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health rights and access to care
rubrics_metrics.description: Health in Angola is rated among the worst globally; a large fraction of the population lacks rudimentary medical attention, and landmines from the civil war continue to cause casualties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure access to healthcare, mortality/morbidity indicators, availability of basic services, and impact of landmines on civilian harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's rights and gender-based violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the constitution guarantees equal rights, societal discrimination is widespread; domestic violence is pervasive, rape (including marital rape) is punishable but under-prosecuted, and sexual harassment is widespread and not explicitly illegal; a law criminalizing domestic violence was passed only in June 2011.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine legislation versus enforcement on gender-based crimes, prevalence of early/child sexual violence, employment restrictions (executive decree barring women from certain jobs), and social practices (witchcraft accusations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraception legality and reproductive rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Contraception is legal in Angola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While legal, assess availability, access, social/cultural barriers, and public-health implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability rights and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrimination against disabled persons is illegal but poorly enforced; there is no law providing for wheelchair access or other protections/services; Angola ratified the CRPD and Optional Protocol in May 2014.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate legal compliance (CRPD ratification), availability of accessibility measures, enforcement of anti-discrimination protections, and prevalence of disability due to landmines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indigenous / traditional peoples' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional hunter-gatherers have little connection to the state; provincial governments are engaged in efforts to improve services, but indigenous groups remain marginalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess state outreach, access to services, recognition of land/rights, and incorporation of traditional dispute resolution in a way that protects rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: LGBT rights (legal status and social treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: As of 2012 the law criminalized same-sex activity (rarely enforced) but a draft penal code recognized same-sex relationships; the constitution defines marriage as between a man and a woman; in 2019 Angola decriminalised homosexuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track changes in law (decriminalization 2019), enforcement history, social harassment incidents, availability of advocacy groups, and legal recognition of relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space for human-rights groups and civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous human-rights groups operate but face government interference, denial of entry to delegates, problems registering, intimidation, harassment, and forced closures (e.g., UNHRO closed Angola office in 2008).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess registration barriers, incidents of entry denial or deportation of delegates/journalists, harassment, and capacity constraints for NGOs.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIV/AIDS rights and stigma
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrimination against persons with HIV/AIDS is illegal but not enforced; people with HIV/AIDS face daily stigma and social exclusion in commerce and social relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure legal protections versus lived experience, prevalence of stigma, enforcement of anti-discrimination rules, and access to treatment and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employees' rights, labor standards, and forced labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Workers may join unions and non-government workers may strike (with strict rules), but collectiv bargaining and workplace protections are weakly enforced; forced labor occurs (including trafficking of men and boys), child labor and exploitation are present, low minimum wage, and occupational health and safety standards are poorly enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate union independence, right to strike in practice, incidence of forced labor/trafficking, child labor statistics, enforcement of labor laws, and workplace safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of refugees and asylum seekers
rubrics_metrics.description: Angolan law allows for granting asylum and refugee status and a system exists for protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practical access to asylum procedures, protection standards, reception conditions, and adherence to international refugee norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of persons under arrest (procedural safeguards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitrary arrest occurs often despite legal prohibitions; warrants are technically required but often not used, about 75% of searches take place without a warrant, prolonged pretrial detention is common, family members sometimes detained, and bribery is used in bail processes; suspects may be informed of charges within five days but right to counsel and prompt judicial review are frequently ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess use of warrants, frequency/duration of pretrial detention, access to counsel (including indigent defense), incidence of bribery/extortion in custody release, and compliance with timelines for court presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of persons on trial and judicial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary is understaffed, inefficient, corrupt, and subject to executive influence (Supreme Court justices appointed by the president for life); defendants are legally entitled to a fair trial but often do not receive one (no juries, limited rights to confront accusers, uneven respect for rights to present witnesses and appeal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine judicial independence, appointment processes, case backlogs, access to prosecutors/magistrates, respect for due process protections, and prevalence of informal/traditional courts substituting for formal justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prisoners' rights and detention conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prison conditions are life-threatening with guards beating and torturing inmates, overcrowding, inadequate food/water/medical care/sanitation, theft/bribery by guards, rape of female inmates, juveniles mixed with adults, and common untreated serious ailments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document detention conditions, incidence of torture/abuse, healthcare availability, segregation of juveniles, monitoring by authorities/NGOs, and official ombudsman activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-order enforcement during emergencies (COVID-19 detentions)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the 2020–21 COVID-19 pandemic police continued to detain people (including for breaching lockdown restrictions), with official figures noting mass short-term detentions (e.g., 295 people in 24 hours in May 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proportionality and legality of pandemic-related detentions, safeguards against arbitrary detention during emergencies, and treatment of detainees.
